lessons.title: ਜੇ (je) — if
lessons.gloss: if - the word that makes a sentence conditional

segments.text: From the chapter behind you, the word that answers why. Two chapters back, the word that sets one clause against another.

segments.instruction: kyoṁki, then par

segments.text: Every joining word so far has taken two things that are true. This one takes something that might not be.
ਜੇ (je) (something that might be so) …

ਜੇ (je) stands at the front of the condition, where English also puts if. That is worth noticing: most of the small words in this book — the postpositions, ਮੈਨੂੰ's ending — come after what they apply to. ਜੇ (je) comes first, and that alone tells the ear a condition is starting.

segments.instruction: je, then any sentence you own.
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *je*, then any sentence you own.]

segments.instruction: the sentence flat, then with je in front.
segments.source: [YOU CONTRAST: the sentence flat, then with *je* in front.]

segments.source: [YOU BUILD: suppose something that might not be true.]

segments.text: Where does ਜੇ (je) stand, and why is that worth noticing? (At the front — most small words in this book come after what they apply to.)

lessons.title: ਜੇ … ਤਾਂ … (je … tāṁ …) — if … then …
lessons.gloss: if... then... - both ends of the condition marked

segments.text: One lesson back, the word that opens a condition. Four chapters back, where ਨਹੀਂ stands.

segments.instruction: je, and nahī̃ before the verb
lekin — from two chapters back

segments.text: Punjabi usually marks both ends:
ਜੇ (je) (condition), ਤਾਂ (result).

English says if it is late, I will go and marks only the front. Punjabi puts ਤਾਂ at the head of the result as well, so the sentence announces its two halves. Beginners often leave it out; it is understood, and the full pair is what you will hear.
The result half is free to be negative, which is where this meets the chapter that opened this run.

segments.instruction: je + a condition, tāṁ + a result.
the same, with the result negative.
segments.source: [YOU BUILD: the same, with the result negative.]

segments.instruction: the pair with tāṁ, then without it.
segments.source: [YOU CONTRAST: the pair with *tāṁ*, then without it.]

segments.text: Make a two-part condition. Which half does English leave unmarked that Punjabi marks? (The result — ਤਾਂ.)

lessons.title: ਜੇ (je) reaches the page
lessons.gloss: if, on two signs already in the hand

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called Script — two signs, neither new until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: One chapter back you wrote ਕਿ and ਕੀ and checked which side each stroke fell on. Write ਕਿ once from memory.
ਜ — ja, ੇ — the laav stroke above.
Set ਅਤੇ, ਜੇ (je) side by side and look only at the top. It is the same laav in both, sitting on different letters. One stroke has now spelled several of this book's most useful words.

blocks.title: Writing — guided copy, model in view

segments.text: Copy ਜੇ (je) once with the model in view, then write it at the front of a line, which is where it belongs.
Write ਜੇ (je) from memory. Which stroke does it share with ਅਤੇ? (The laav above.)

lessons.title: ਜਦੋਂ (jadoṁ) — when
lessons.gloss: when - locating one event against another

needs: your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down. You can listen to all of it now and come back to the parts that need looking at once you have stopped.

segments.text: One lesson back you wrote ਜੇ (je). And before that, the two-part condition.

segments.instruction: ਜੇ, and je … tāṁ …
the pair rule — from two chapters back
segments.source: [YOU RECALL: the pair rule — from two chapters back]

segments.text: ਜਦੋਂ (jadoṁ) (one event), (the other).
ਜਦੋਂ (jadoṁ) sets two events against each other in time. Like ਜੇ (je), it opens its clause rather than following it — and look at the front of both words. The same ਜ.

That is not a coincidence. Punjabi builds a family of clause-openers on that one letter, the way it builds its questions on ਕ. You now own two members of it, and the pattern is worth more than either word alone.

segments.instruction: jadoṁ + an event, then a second event.
segments.source: [YOU BUILD: *jadoṁ* + an event, then a second event.]

segments.instruction: je and jadoṁ on the same two clauses — one supposes, one times.
segments.source: [YOU CONTRAST: *je* and *jadoṁ* on the same two clauses — one supposes, one times.]

segments.instruction: the shared ਜ at the front of both.
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the shared **ਜ** at the front of both.]

segments.text: Say a when sentence. What do ਜੇ (je) and ਜਦੋਂ (jadoṁ) share, and what does it mark? (The opening ਜ — a family of clause-openers.)

lessons.title: ਲਈ (laī) — for, in order to
lessons.gloss: for, in order to - the reason stated forwards

segments.text: One lesson back, the word that times one event against another. One chapter back, the word that answers why.

segments.instruction: jadoṁ, and kyoṁki
the contrast kit — from two chapters back
segments.source: [YOU RECALL: the contrast kit — from two chapters back]

segments.text: ਕਿਉਂਕਿ looks backwards — it names the cause of something that already happened. ਲਈ (laī) looks forwards — it names what something is for:
(a thing) ਲਈ (laī) — "for …"

And notice where it stands. ਜੇ (je) and ਜਦੋਂ (jadoṁ) open their clauses; ਲਈ (laī) follows what it applies to, like the postpositions this book taught long ago. Two habits, and the word tells you which one it belongs to by where it sits.
Cause and purpose are different answers to the same why, and a language that used one word for both would make its learners guess. Punjabi does not.

segments.instruction: something you can name, then laī.
segments.source: [YOU SAY: something you can name, then *laī*.]

segments.instruction: a kyoṁki answer and a laī answer to the same question.
segments.source: [YOU CONTRAST: a *kyoṁki* answer and a *laī* answer to the same question.]

segments.instruction: je at the front, laī at the back.
segments.source: [YOU CONTRAST: *je* at the front, *laī* at the back.]

segments.text: Which of ਕਿਉਂਕਿ and ਲਈ (laī) looks back at a cause, and which forward to a purpose? Where does each stand? Next chapter: he, we, and the word for the one who.
